patients.summary: Retired postal worker with CAD after a 2016 STEMI and stent, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia and CKD 3b who joins in 2020. Ischemic cardiomyopathy with an LV aneurysm and HFrEF are found in 2022, followed by three admissions (decompensation after running out of pills, flash pulmonary edema, hyponatremia to 118) and a PEA arrest in April 2026 that he survives intact.

documents.title: New patient call
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Mr. Marino called asking to join the practice. Retired from the post office, on Medicare, says his old doctor's office is closing its panel to Medicare patients and he would rather move now than wait. Explained the membership model and the fee; he and his wife already talked it over. Booked a new patient visit 9/14 at 9:00 (60 min). Records release signed over the phone, faxed to his prior primary care office today with request for last 5 years of notes, labs, hospital records and immunizations. Asked him to bring all his pill bottles.

documents.title: Records from prior primary care office
documents.author: MA
documents.body:
Fax received, 41 pages, from his previous primary care office. Scanned to chart. Abstract for the new patient visit:

Problem list on their records: hypertension; type 2 diabetes; hyperlipidemia; coronary artery disease; history of STEMI 2016; coronary stent; chronic kidney disease stage 3.

Cardiac: hospital discharge paperwork from May 2016 included in the packet. Admitted through an outside emergency department with an ST-elevation MI, taken for PCI with one drug-eluting stent. Discharged on aspirin, a beta blocker, an ACE inhibitor and a high-intensity statin. Later office notes say he finished the second antiplatelet agent after a year.

Med list as of their last visit (06/2020): aspirin 81 mg daily, metoprolol succinate ER 50 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice a day.

Screening: colonoscopy 2014, normal exam, repeat in 10 years.
Immunizations listed: flu shots most years, last 10/2019. No pneumococcal or shingles vaccine documented.
Allergies: NKDA.

Originals filed under Media.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT

CC: transferring care.

HPI: 65M here to establish. Retired letter carrier, 30-some years walking a route, retired in 2019. Comes with a bag of bottles and a typed med list his wife made. Feels well. Walks most days, no limitation. No chest pain since his heart attack. Prior office records reviewed (fax 9/3): STEMI in May 2016 at an outside hospital, PCI with a single drug-eluting stent, finished dual antiplatelet therapy after a year. Diabetes since about 2011, on metformin only, never on insulin. Kidney function has been 'a little off' for a couple of years per his old doctor. Has not seen cardiology in a few years; says the group told him to follow up as needed once he was stable.

PMH: HTN, HLD, T2DM, CAD s/p STEMI and DES 2016, CKD 3.
PSH: PCI with stent 2016.
Meds (bottles reconciled): aspirin 81 daily, metoprolol succinate 50 daily, lisinopril 20 daily, atorvastatin 40 daily, metformin 1000 BID.
Allergies: NKDA.
FH: father had CAD, MI at 62. Mother T2DM and HTN. Older brother high cholesterol.
SH: married, lives with his wife. Never smoked. Doesn't drink. No drugs.
Screening: colonoscopy 2014 normal per records.

ROS: negative in detail, including no dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, claudication, urinary symptoms, numbness in feet.

Exam: well-appearing, pleasant. Neck no JVD, no bruits. Heart RRR, normal S1 S2, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. Ext no edema, DP and PT pulses 2+ bilaterally. Feet: skin intact, no calluses, monofilament sensation intact both feet. Neuro grossly nonfocal.

A/P:
1. HTN: a touch above goal today, rechecked similar. Continue lisinopril 20, metoprolol. Home cuff readings next visit.
2. T2DM: A1c today. Continue metformin. Foot exam normal. Needs a diabetic eye exam; gave him the optometry list.
3. CAD s/p STEMI/DES: asymptomatic. Continue aspirin, beta blocker, statin.
4. HLD: lipid panel today.
5. CKD 3b by his old labs: CMP, urine albumin today. Avoid NSAIDs, discussed.
6. HM: hep C and HIV screen today (once). Flu shot next month when the high-dose arrives. Pneumococcal and shingles discussed, will plan. Colonoscopy due 2024.
RTC 3 months.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Mr. Marino, your labs from Monday are back. Your A1c is 7.7, a little above where I'd like it; let's recheck in March after the holidays. LDL cholesterol is 69, good on the atorvastatin. Kidney function is in the same range your old office was seeing, stage 3, and your urine protein test is normal. Hepatitis C and HIV screens were negative. Blood counts normal. No changes for now. See you in December.

MEDICARE ANNUAL WELLNESS VISIT (initial)

Health risk assessment reviewed with patient. Lives with wife in a two-story house, bedroom upstairs, no trouble with stairs. Independent with all daily activities, still drives, does the yard. No falls in the past year. Hearing fine per him, wife disagrees mildly; he declines audiology for now. Vision: eye exam in August, no retinopathy, new glasses. Sleeps 7 hours.

Depression screen PHQ-2: 0.
Cognition: Mini-Cog 5/5.
Activity: walks 30-40 min most days.
Diet: wife cooks, cutting back on bread and pasta 'mostly'.

Medications reviewed, no changes. No OTC NSAIDs.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: BP and weight reviewed. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Feet normal, monofilament intact bilaterally, pulses good.

Screening/prevention plan:
- Colon: colonoscopy 2014 normal, due 2024.

- Shingrix #1 today, #2 in 2-6 months.
- Pneumococcal: PCV20 with flu shot in October.

orders.reason: Exertional dyspnea and orthopnea in a patient with CAD after STEMI

documents.title: Office Visit - Dyspnea
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: getting winded.

HPI: Since mid-July has been short of breath on his walks, now stops halfway up the hill on his street that he used to do without a break. More tired in general. For the past few weeks has been sleeping on 3 pillows because he feels breathless flat; wife noticed. No chest pain or pressure, no palpitations, no fainting or near-fainting. No cough, fever, leg swelling he has noticed. No change in meds, taking all of them.

History: CAD with STEMI and DES 2016, HTN, DM2, HLD, CKD 3b. Has not seen cardiology since about 2017.

Exam: Sitting comfortably, speaks full sentences. BP and HR as recorded, SpO2 normal at rest. No JVD at 45 degrees. Heart RRR, no gallop. Lungs clear to bases. Abdomen soft. No ankle or leg edema.

A/P:
Exertional dyspnea and orthopnea, about 7 weeks, in a man with a prior MI. Worry about a cardiac cause, i.e. LV dysfunction or ischemia, even without angina.
- Cardiology referral, asked for the next available new consult with echo. Front desk to push for within 6 weeks.
- Start furosemide 40 mg every morning for the orthopnea in the meantime.
- BMP and CBC today, BMP again in 2 weeks on the diuretic.
- Precautions: chest pain, worsening breathlessness at rest, swelling, fainting -> call or 911.
RTC after cardiology.

documents.author: RN
documents.body: Per PCP, called patient: potassium and kidney function stable on the water pill, no change. Confirmed cardiology appointment Oct 19 at 1:30 with echo the same afternoon; he has the address and will bring his med list. He asked if he can keep taking the furosemide in the morning only, told him yes.

documents.title: Fall vaccines
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Flu high-dose IM R deltoid, COVID bivalent (Pfizer) IM L deltoid. Screening negative. Observed 15 min, no reaction. Pt says breathing 'about the same,' sleeping propped up; he has cardiology 10/19. Encouraged him to keep it.

conditions.label: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

reports.text:
Indication: exertional dyspnea, prior myocardial infarction.
Technically adequate study.
Left ventricle: dilated. Akinesis of the anterior wall and the septum. Remaining segments contract. Left ventricular ejection fraction 35%.
Right ventricle: normal size and systolic function.
Atria: normal size.
Valves: aortic valve trileaflet, opens normally. Mitral leaflets structurally normal. Tricuspid and pulmonic valves normal.
Pericardium: no effusion.
IVC: normal size with normal respiratory variation.
reports.conclusion: Dilated left ventricle with anterior and septal akinesis; LVEF 35%.

reports.text: Sinus rhythm, rate 78. Persistent ST-segment elevation in the anterior leads with deep Q waves.
reports.conclusion: Sinus rhythm; anterior Q waves with persistent ST elevation.

documents.title: Cardiology consultation letter
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE CARDIOLOGY GROUP - NEW PATIENT CONSULTATION
Date of visit: 10/19/2022
Re: Howard Marino, DOB 01/19/1955

Dear Doctor,

Thank you for asking us to see Mr. Marino, a 67-year-old retired postal worker with coronary disease (STEMI 2016 treated with a drug-eluting stent), hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia and stage 3 kidney disease, about breathlessness.

Over roughly three months he has noticed steadily worsening shortness of breath with exertion and more fatigue, and he now needs to sleep propped up. He has had no chest pain, no palpitations and no syncope. You started furosemide in September.

Medications: aspirin 81 mg, metoprolol succinate 50 mg, lisinopril 20 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, furosemide 40 mg daily.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Family history: father with coronary disease and an MI at 62; mother diabetic and hypertensive; older brother with high cholesterol.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol. Retired from the postal service.

Exam: BP 130/80, heart rate 78, respiratory rate 20. On auscultation there is a holosystolic murmur at the apex that radiates to the axilla. Lungs are clear. No peripheral edema.

ECG: sinus rhythm with persistent anterior ST elevation and deep Q waves.
Echocardiogram today: the left ventricle is dilated, the anterior wall and septum are akinetic, and the ejection fraction is 35%.

Impression:
1. Ischemic cardiomyopathy with a left ventricular aneurysm involving the anterior wall and septum, the late result of his 2016 infarct.
2. Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
3. Coronary artery disease, stented 2016, no angina.

Plan: continue aspirin, metoprolol succinate, lisinopril, atorvastatin and furosemide as he takes them. Daily weights, 2 g sodium diet, call for a gain of more than 3 pounds in a day or 5 in a week. We will see him again in the spring.

Thank you for the referral.

Cardiology

documents.title: Annual Wellness Visit

How he is doing: breathlessness on hills unchanged, sleeps on 2-3 pillows. Weighing himself every morning now, steady. Salt: wife has stopped using the shaker and they are reading labels.

HRA: lives with wife, independent, drives, no falls. PHQ-2 0. Mini-Cog normal last year, no concerns.

Meds: aspirin 81, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40, metformin 1000 BID, furosemide 40 qAM.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: Heart regular, no S3 heard today, apical systolic murmur noted as in the cardiology letter. Lungs clear. No edema. Feet intact, monofilament normal.

Plan:
- HFrEF/ICM: continue per cardiology. Daily weights, sodium limit. Reviewed when to call.
- DM2: A1c today.
- CKD 3b: CMP, urine albumin.
- HTN controlled.
- Prevention: flu and COVID done 10/4. Colonoscopy due 2024. PSA declined again. Shingrix, Tdap, PCV20 complete.
- Advance directive: still thinking.
RTC 3 months.

documents.title: Emergency department record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT - PHYSICIAN RECORD
Date of service: 04/06/2023, 21:15
Patient: Howard Marino, 68 M

Chief complaint: shortness of breath x 2 days, can't lie flat, legs swollen.

HPI: 68-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy with LV aneurysm and chronic systolic heart failure, seen by cardiology about six months ago for progressive dyspnea. Over two days he has become so breathless that walking across his bedroom winds him, and he has spent the last two nights sleeping sitting up in a chair. Feet and lower legs have swollen up. He ran out of his furosemide and his lisinopril roughly a week ago and had not gotten them refilled.

PMH: CAD with prior MI and PCI/DES; chronic systolic HF; DM2; hyperlipidemia; HTN; CKD 3.
Home meds (still taking): aspirin 81, metoprolol succinate 50, atorvastatin 40, metformin 1000 BID. Out of furosemide and lisinopril x ~1 week.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: no tobacco, no alcohol.

Exam: BP 102/68, HR 106, RR 26. Looks tired and is mildly confused. JVD up to the angle of the jaw. Crackles across both lung bases. Apical impulse displaced laterally; S3 present. Moderate pitting edema of both legs.

ECG: sinus tachycardia, inferior Q waves.
CXR: big heart, vascular congestion, Kerley B lines.

ED course: oxygen by nasal cannula. IV furosemide. Cardiology and ICU contacted; pulmonary artery catheter placed for hemodynamic monitoring.

Impression: acute on chronic systolic heart failure, decompensated, after running out of diuretic and ACE inhibitor.
Disposition: admitted to the cardiac ICU.

events.reason: Acute on chronic systolic heart failure

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: hospitalist
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 04/06/2023 (via ED)   Discharged: 04/11/2023
Attending service: Cardiology

Principal diagnosis: acute on chronic systolic (reduced EF) heart failure.
Precipitant: ran out of furosemide and lisinopril about one week before admission.
Other: ischemic cardiomyopathy with LV aneurysm; CAD s/p PCI; type 2 diabetes; hypertension; hyperlipidemia; CKD stage 3.

Hospital course: Admitted to the cardiac ICU from the ED in decompensated heart failure, tachycardic, with a pulmonary artery catheter placed in the ED. Diuresed with IV furosemide guided by the catheter numbers. Breathing improved over the first 48 hours and his confusion cleared. Catheter removed on hospital day 3 and he moved to the cardiac floor. Home lisinopril restarted once pressures allowed and changed back to oral furosemide 40 mg daily before discharge. Walking the halls without oxygen at discharge.

Discharge medications (no changes from his prior regimen):
- aspirin 81 mg daily
- metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily
- lisinopril 20 mg daily
- atorvastatin 40 mg daily
- metformin 1000 mg twice daily
- furosemide 40 mg every morning

Allergies: NKDA.
Instructions: daily weights, 2 g sodium, do not let prescriptions lapse. Follow up with PCP within 7 days and with cardiology.

documents.title: Post-discharge nurse call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Called within 2 business days of discharge. Spoke with patient and his wife on speaker. Home since Tuesday. Breathing much better, sleeping in bed on 2 pillows. Weight this morning 190 lb. Has all six meds in hand; wife picked up furosemide and lisinopril from the local pharmacy the day he came home. Reviewed: daily weight, call if up 3 lb in a day or 5 in a week, or if the breathlessness comes back. Gave him our number for refills in the future, we can bridge locally. TCM visit booked 4/19.

documents.title: Transitional Care Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
TCM visit. Discharge summary and ED record reviewed (admitted 4/6-4/11, decompensated HFrEF after a week without furosemide and lisinopril; PA catheter, IV diuresis, regimen resumed unchanged).

He feels 'like before.' Back to walking the street, not the hill yet. Sleeps on 2 pillows. No swelling. Home weights 189-190.

Med reconciliation against the discharge list: all six present, matched bottle by bottle. Moved his refills to auto-ship and set every med to the same 90-day cycle. Wife is adding the refill date to the fridge calendar.

Exam: Alert, oriented, conversational. Weight down from his pre-admission baseline. JVP flat. Heart regular, soft apical systolic murmur, no S3. Lungs clear. No edema.

A/P:
1. HFrEF, recent decompensation from medication lapse: euvolemic today. Continue current doses. BMP today after the IV diuresis. Cardiology follow-up in June already booked.
2. CKD 3b: check creatinine.
3. DM2, HTN, CAD: unchanged.
RTC July.

documents.title: Post-hospital BMP
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Creatinine 1.9 after diuresis, a little above his 1.8. Potassium and sodium fine. Will recheck in July; no change today.

documents.title: Cardiology follow-up letter
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Cardiology follow-up, 06/14/2023
Re: Howard Marino

Dear Doctor,

I saw Mr. Marino after his April admission for decompensated heart failure, which followed a week off furosemide and lisinopril. He is back to his usual activity. Mild breathlessness on inclines. Sleeps on two pillows. No chest pain, palpitations or lightheadedness. Weights steady.

Medications: aspirin 81 mg, metoprolol succinate 50 mg, lisinopril 20 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, metformin 1000 mg BID, furosemide 40 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: comfortable. Apical systolic murmur unchanged. Lungs clear. No edema.

Assessment: ischemic cardiomyopathy with LV aneurysm, HFrEF, euvolemic on his current regimen. CAD without angina.
Plan: no changes. We stressed the importance of never running out of the diuretic. Return in one year, sooner if needed.

Sincerely,
Cardiology

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT RECORD - regional hospital
Arrival 04/08/2024 04:10 by ambulance
Howard Marino, 69-year-old male

CC: can't breathe.

HPI: Known ischemic cardiomyopathy with LV aneurysm and HFrEF, admitted here in April 2023 for decompensation. Severe shortness of breath came on suddenly over the past several hours. His ankles have been getting progressively more swollen over the past week, and lately he has had more trouble lying flat at night. Similar to last year's episode but faster.

PMH: longstanding HTN, CAD with prior MI and stent, HFrEF, DM2, HLD, CKD 3.
Meds: aspirin 81, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40, metformin 1000 BID, furosemide 40. Taking them per patient.
Allergies: NKDA.
SH: never smoker, no alcohol. Retired postal worker.

Exam: RR 32, SpO2 86% on room air, BP 168/102, HR 112. Anxious and sweaty. JVD present. Crackles throughout both lung fields. S3 gallop.

CXR: diffuse alveolar infiltrates, bilateral effusions.

Assessment: acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary edema.

ED course: placed on supplemental oxygen, IV furosemide, nesiritide infusion started. Admitted to the step-down unit.

events.reason: Acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary edema

documents.author: hospitalist
documents.body:
Discharge Summary
Admission 4/8/2024 - Discharge 4/12/2024

Diagnosis: acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary edema (HFrEF, ischemic cardiomyopathy with LV aneurysm).
Comorbid: CAD s/p stent, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, CKD 3.

Course: Came in with abrupt-onset pulmonary edema and hypoxemia (SpO2 86% RA) and a BP of 168/102. Treated with a nesiritide infusion and IV furosemide in the step-down unit. Oxygen weaned to room air by day 3. Nesiritide stopped day 2. Converted to oral furosemide. Ambulating independently at discharge.

Discharge medications - unchanged:
aspirin 81 mg daily; metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily; lisinopril 20 mg daily; atorvastatin 40 mg daily; metformin 1000 mg BID; furosemide 40 mg daily.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.

Follow-up: primary care within one week; cardiology as scheduled. Daily weights, sodium restriction.

documents.author: RN
documents.body: TCM call. Discharged Friday 4/12. Pt says he is 'tired but breathing fine.' Weight 190 this am. Has all meds, nothing new or stopped per his discharge sheet. No swelling. Sleeping in bed. Reviewed weight rules and 911 for sudden breathlessness. Visit Thursday 4/18 confirmed; wife will drive.

Post-hospital visit. ED record and discharge summary reviewed: 4/8-4/12, sudden pulmonary edema with hypoxemia, BP 168/102 on arrival, treated with nesiritide and IV furosemide; regimen unchanged at discharge.

This time he had not run out of anything; bottles checked, counts match. Swelling had crept up over a week and he didn't call. He knows now.

Today: tired, short of breath only on stairs. 2 pillows. Weight at home 189-190.

Exam: no distress. BP at goal today. JVP not elevated. Heart regular, apical systolic murmur, no gallop. Lungs clear. No edema.

Med rec: aspirin 81, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40, metformin 1000 BID, furosemide 40. Matches discharge.

1. HFrEF s/p 2nd admission: euvolemic. Continue. Call for 3 lb/day or 5 lb/week gain or ankle swelling. Cardiology 6/12.

3. CKD 3b: BMP.
RTC July.

DOS 04/18/2025 15:40
Pt: Howard Marino, 70 y/o M

CC: confused per neighbor.

HPI: 70-year-old with ischemic cardiomyopathy and HFrEF, seen here for heart failure decompensations in 2023 and 2024, brought in after a neighbor found him confused and disoriented. He can tell us his name but not the date or where he is, and he can't give much of his history. No family member came with him. The neighbor says he has been drinking less water lately because he is afraid of having to get up at night to use the bathroom.

PMH (from our records): ischemic cardiomyopathy with LV aneurysm, HFrEF, CAD s/p MI and stent, HTN, DM2, HLD, CKD 3.
Meds per our last list: aspirin 81, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40, metformin 1000 BID, furosemide 40.
Allergies: NKDA.
Advance directive: none on file. No designated surrogate.

Exam: BP 160/90, HR 88, RR 18, T 37.1 C (98.8 F). Skin warm and dry. Disoriented to time and place. No focal neurological deficits.

Labs: Na 118, K 4.5, Cl 88, HCO3 24, glucose 180, creatinine 2.1 (baseline 1.9). Serum osmolality 250. Urine sodium low.

Impression: acute confusion with severe hypotonic hyponatremia.
Plan: admit to medicine, careful sodium correction with frequent checks, hold free water, neuro checks.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: hospitalist
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY - Medicine
Admit 04/18/2025   Discharge 04/22/2025

Principal problem: hyponatremia (Na 118 on arrival) with acute confusion.
Chronic: HFrEF / ischemic cardiomyopathy with LV aneurysm; CAD s/p stent; HTN; DM2; HLD; CKD 3 (creatinine 2.1 on arrival vs baseline 1.9).

Hospital course: Sodium raised slowly with frequent checks, staying within safe daily limits. Confusion lifted over the first two days; by day 3 he was oriented and back to his usual self per his wife, who visited daily. Sodium 131 on the morning of discharge. Diuretic plan discussed: take the furosemide in the morning so it is done before bedtime, and drink normally rather than cutting fluids to avoid night trips.

Discharge meds (unchanged): aspirin 81 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg BID, furosemide 40 mg every morning.
Allergies: NKDA.

documents.title: Emergency department resuscitation record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Resuscitation record, 04/12/2026, arrival 18:25 by EMS
Howard Marino, 71 M

History (from wife and EMS): 71-year-old man with CAD, hypertension and ischemic cardiomyopathy with LV aneurysm, with repeated heart failure admissions. His wife found him unresponsive at home this evening. Earlier in the day he had told her he was short of breath and had chest pain, but he would not agree to come in.

Meds per wife: aspirin, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40, metformin, furosemide 40.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol, retired postal worker.

On arrival: pulseless and apneic. Monitor shows an organized rhythm with no palpable pulse (PEA).

Interventions: intubated; CPR continued; IV access obtained; epinephrine given. Return of spontaneous circulation after further CPR and epinephrine.

Initial labs: Na 140, K 4.2, Cl 102, HCO3 24, BUN 18, glucose 180. Troponin I pending at the time of this note. ABG on 100% FiO2: pH 7.1, PaCO2 60, PaO2 500.

Impression: cardiac arrest, PEA, with ROSC.
Disposition: ICU, intubated.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: hospitalist
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 04/12/2026 via ED to the medical ICU; transferred to the cardiac floor 04/17/2026; discharged 04/22/2026.

Principal diagnosis: cardiac arrest (PEA) with return of spontaneous circulation in the ED.
Secondary: ischemic cardiomyopathy with LV aneurysm and HFrEF; old MI; CAD on antiplatelet therapy, stent 2016; essential hypertension; type 2 diabetes with stress hyperglycemia on arrival (glucose 180); hyperlipidemia; CKD stage 3.

Course:
ICU: post-arrest care on the ventilator. He woke appropriately and was extubated on 04/14. Troponin I rose and then fell over the first two days, felt to reflect the arrest and the resuscitation. Neurologically intact on serial exams.
Cardiology: coronary angiography 04/16 showed the 2016 stent patent and no new obstructive lesion. The arrest was attributed to his ischemic cardiomyopathy.
Floor: walked with physical therapy, cleared for home without services.

Discharge medications (no changes from home):
aspirin 81 mg daily; metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily; lisinopril 20 mg daily; atorvastatin 40 mg daily; metformin 1000 mg twice daily; furosemide 40 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.

Discharged home with his wife. Follow-up: PCP within 7 days; cardiology within 1 month. Call 911 for chest pain or breathlessness, and do not wait.

documents.title: Post-discharge nurse call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: TCM call 2 days after discharge. Spoke with wife, then patient. Home, tired, sleeping a lot. No chest pain like before, breathing okay at rest. Meds the same six; wife has the pillbox set. Weight 183 lb. Cardiology appointment 5/13. Reinforced: any chest pain or shortness of breath means 911, not waiting. Visit with PCP 4/29, wife will come.

conditions.label: Personal history of sudden cardiac arrest

documents.title: Transitional Care Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
TCM visit after cardiac arrest. ED resuscitation record and discharge summary reviewed: found unresponsive by his wife 4/12 after chest pain and breathlessness earlier that day that he did not report; PEA arrest, intubated, CPR and epinephrine with ROSC in the ED; extubated 4/14; troponin rose and fell; cath 4/16 with a patent stent and no new blockage; arrest attributed to his cardiomyopathy. Home 4/22, meds unchanged.

He and his wife both here. He remembers nothing from that afternoon until the ICU. Walking around the house and to the mailbox. No chest pain since. Short of breath on stairs, about as before. Sleeping well.

He said, unprompted, that he should have let her call. We talked through it: chest pain or new breathlessness means 911.

Med rec: aspirin 81, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40, metformin 1000 BID, furosemide 40 qAM. Matches discharge.

Exam: thinner. Alert, oriented, clear speech, memory for recent events intact apart from the arrest day. Heart regular, apical holosystolic murmur. Lungs clear. No edema.

A/P
1. Cardiac arrest (PEA), survived neurologically intact: resolved; problem list now carries it as history. Cardiology 5/13.
2. HFrEF/ICM: euvolemic, continue.
3. CKD 3b, DM2, HTN: BMP and CBC today.
4. Health care proxy: they want to do this properly now. Booked a visit 5/21 for it.
RTC 5/21.

Plan: continue the current regimen. Return in three months.
